newsitem.title: USA: American could survive lengthy strike.
newsitem.headline: American could survive lengthy strike.

text.p: American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp, could survive a pilot strike of about 42 days before falling into the red for the year, but most industry analysts expect the threatened strike to last less than a week.
While American's stock likely would be slammed initially if the strike goes ahead, that weakness could open a buying opportunity if the strike is quickly resolved, analysts said.
AMR Corp executives and union officials have been negotiating in Washington as a Feb 15 strike deadline looms. The pilots union said Thursday it made a new proposal in attempts to avert a strike.

Timothy Ross, an airline analyst with SBC Warburg, expects AMR's stock could plunge up to 15 percent immediately following the start of a strike, based on an expected strike duration of about four to five days.
If the strike lasts more than a week, all bets are off, analysts said.
Ross said he upgraded the stock to a buy from an "add" rating, due to weakness in the share price since the pilots rejected the airline's wage offer in January.
AMR was trading up 7/8 at 83-3/4, compared to 88-1/8 at the end of 1996.
American's Chairman Robert Crandall claims a three month strike would destroy the carrier. But American is better positioned to weather a strike than other airlines in the past, analysts said.

The airline has lined up $2 billion in borrowed funds to help it survive a possible strike. The company is also flush with more than $1 billion in profits generated in 1996, up from $162 million in profits the year before.
"With that cash on hand, American could last a long time until they run into liquidity problems," said Jeffrey Long, an analyst with J.P. Morgan Securities.
Most industry analysts said the strike could cost more than $20 million a day. The pilots' union officials said the costs could rise up to $40 million a day, or about $1.2 billion a month.
At that rate, American's expected 1997 profits would be wiped out in about 42 days, analysts said.
If the strike lingers, AMR could lose market share as other airlines pick up their customers. American's cargo unit could also suffer as clients find other carriers to ship goods.
"It may take a while to regain market share if competitors shift capacity in certain markets," Long said.
UAL Corp unit United Airlines' 1985 strike "left a door open at Chicago for American to gain the dominance they have there today," he said.
